skincare-skin-cycling.text: Skin cycling is used to get retinoid and exfoliant benefits for tone and texture while giving the skin barrier recovery nights. It spread through TikTok skincare circles. The rotation follows dermatology convention, but the schedule itself has not been trialled.

oral-antibiotics-doxycycline-minocycline.text: Users in acne circles take prescribed doxycycline or minocycline to calm inflammatory breakouts and reduce red, active lesions for clearer skin. Their use in acne is established in dermatology, with trials supporting it.

topical-clindamycin.text: Prescribed clindamycin gel or lotion is used, usually alongside benzoyl peroxide, to reduce mild to moderate inflammatory breakouts and get clearer skin. Its use in acne is well studied in clinical trials.

dapsone-gel-aczone.text: Dapsone gel is a prescription topical that acne forum posters use to calm inflamed breakouts, often as an alternative when other topicals irritate. Large phase 3 trials have studied it specifically for acne.

sarecycline-seysara.text: Sarecycline is a once-daily prescription tetracycline that people with moderate to severe inflammatory acne take to clear facial and body breakouts. It was approved for that use in 2018 and has been studied in acne trials.

combined-oral-contraceptive-pill.text: Women use the combined pill, prescribed off its main contraceptive purpose, to reduce hormonal acne by lowering androgen activity and sebum. Its use for acne is studied and recognised in dermatology.

chain: Clear skin with fewer side effects
low-dose-isotretinoin-microdosing-accuta.text: Forum posters discuss taking small continuous isotretinoin amounts instead of a full course to keep acne away with milder side effects, sometimes as maintenance after a course. Low-dose regimens have been studied in acne, but online protocols are mostly anecdotal.

spearmint-tea.text: Spearmint tea is drunk by people with hormonal acne who hope it lowers androgens and clears breakouts. One small trial looked at androgen levels in PCOS; acne itself has not been tested.

low-glycemic-diet-for-acne.text: Acne-prone users eat low-glycemic carbohydrates hoping to reduce breakouts by lowering insulin and sebum signalling. It is the diet change with the most trial support for acne, though the evidence is modest.

fungal-acne-protocol-malassezia.text: People with stubborn, itchy forehead or body bumps avoid fatty-acid oils and use antifungal washes aiming to clear them. Malassezia folliculitis is a recognised condition treated with antifungals, though self-diagnosis in forums is common.

double-cleansing.text: Skincare communities use an oil cleanser followed by a foaming cleanser in the evening to fully remove sunscreen, makeup and oil for clearer skin. The routine comes from Korean and Japanese beauty practice and has not been trialled.

skin-cycling.text: Skin cycling is used for acne, scars, fine lines and glow by rotating acid and retinoid nights with recovery nights, and is promoted for sensitive or acne-prone skin. It was popularised by a dermatologist and TikTok; the schedule itself has not been trialled.

oil-cleansing-method.text: Users massage plant oils into the face to dissolve sebum, makeup and sunscreen, aiming for clearer, brighter skin and sometimes fewer breakouts. It is popular and debated in acne circles, and the method itself has not been trialled.

chemical-peels-for-acne.text: Salicylic, glycolic and Jessner peels are used in clinics and at home to clear acne, reduce oil, and fade marks and scars. Small studies exist for acne, while guidelines describe the evidence as insufficient.

chain: Light activates photosensitizer in oil glands
photodynamic-therapy-ala-pdt.text: People with severe or stubborn acne pursue ALA-PDT in clinics to target oil glands and inflamed lesions, sometimes on the body too. Some trials and a review report benefit for acne, with mixed results.

chain: Manual removal of blackheads and whiteheads
professional-extractions-acne-facial.text: An esthetician or dermatologist manually clears blackheads and whiteheads, giving visibly cleaner pores right after the session. It is standard acne facial practice, with little formal trial evidence on long-term outcomes.

chain: Swelling drops within a day or two
intralesional-cortisone-injection.text: People with a large painful cyst before an event get a clinician to inject cortisone, commonly described as shrinking it overnight. The visible flattening is widely reported in appearance communities; trial detail was not covered in the sources reviewed.

toothpaste-on-pimples.text: People dab toothpaste on a pimple overnight, saying it dries the spot out. This is a long-running home remedy based on anecdote; no studies were found, and toothpaste is not formulated for skin.

apple-cider-vinegar-toner.text: Home-remedy fans apply diluted apple cider vinegar as a toner for acne and oily skin. The idea rests on its acidity and anecdotes, and no studies were found on its use for acne.

chain: Acid and vitamin C on blemish
lemon-juice-on-pimples.text: Proponents dab lemon juice on pimples and dark marks, citing its acidity and vitamin C. The use is based on home-remedy tradition, and no studies were found on it for acne.

aspirin-mask.text: Users crush aspirin into a paste and apply it to the face for acne and redness, reasoning from aspirin's relation to salicylic acid. Salicylic acid itself is studied for acne; the aspirin mask has not been.

honey-mask-manuka.text: Skincare fans apply manuka honey as a mask to calm skin and clear breakouts. Honey has been studied in wound care, but no acne studies were found.

bentonite-clay-mask.text: People with oily or congested skin use wash-off bentonite clay masks to soak up oil for a less shiny, cleaner-looking face. The cosmetic claims rest on the clay's absorbency and common use; no clinical trials were found.

vitamin-b5-pantothenic-acid-high-dose.text: Skincare and looksmaxxing posters take very high-dose vitamin B5 hoping to reduce skin oil and acne. The theory draws on its role in fatty acid metabolism; no acne trials were found.

probiotics-for-acne.text: Acne-prone users take oral probiotics or use topical ones based on the gut-skin axis and the skin microbiome. Reviews and trials exist, but the evidence is preliminary and strain-specific.

dim-supplement.text: Used off-label for hormonal acne, DIM is taken by users who want to change estrogen and androgen balance for clearer skin. The research on DIM concerns hormones and cancer; acne has not been studied.

hypochlorous-acid-spray.text: Acne-prone users mist hypochlorous acid on face or body to reduce bacteria and soothe irritation. It is established in wound and eyelid care; its appearance use for acne has not been tested.

accure-laser-1726-nm.text: Accure is an in-office 1726 nm laser used to shrink the oil glands behind persistent acne, similar to Aviclear. Registered trials exist, but published results were not found in the sources reviewed.

chain: Vacuum clears pores, light hits bacteria
isolaz-pulsed-light-acne-treatment.text: Isolaz is a clinic treatment combining suction and pulsed light, discussed in looksmaxxing circles for clogged pores and acne-prone skin. Public evidence behind it is thin.

sun-exposure-for-acne.text: Some people sit in the sun or tan hoping to dry out blemishes, and report short-term improvement in how skin looks. Reference sources link sun exposure to lingering dark marks rather than clearer skin.
